https://www.dw.com/en/us-new-york-city-m.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5KhUu Mamdani said AI-powered early education is not inevitable Image: NDZ/STAR MAX/IPx/picture alliance Advertisement New York City public schools will temporarily bar elementary and middle school students from using generative artificial intelligence tools during the upcoming school year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Wednesday. Officials have described this as the most expansive such prohibition in the United States . What do we know about the AI ban? The one-year moratorium bars student-facing generative AI software for students through eighth grade, affecting roughly 600,000 public school students, while officials study how children use the technology. The city said the policy will halt use of about 40 educational AI tools currently used in classrooms.. Companion chatbots will be banned across all grade levels. However, high schoolers will be exempt from the full ban. The city will roll out twice-yearly AI literacy classes for all public high school students and launch pilot programs letting some use select AI platforms under teacher supervision. Teachers, meanwhile, will still be permitted to use AI for lesson planning and administrative tasks such as scheduling. What did Mayor Mamdani say about the restrictions? Mamdani framed the decision around the value of human connection in education : "Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow. They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators and wrestle with tough problems on their own." He also tied the policy to the district's broader teaching ideals, saying, "Each day when our children come to school, we teach them to ask questions, to challenge assumptions, to interrogate the premise, to ask why. When it comes to AI in our schools, we hold an obligation to do the same." New York's move comes as school districts across the country weigh the benefits and risks of generative AI in classrooms. AI knows what you did last summer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Is New York alone in banning AI? New York's move comes as school districts across the country weigh the benefits and risks of generative AI in classrooms. One of the largest examples is Los Angeles Unified, the US's second-largest school district, which is also temporarily blocking generative AI tools on student devices across all grades as it develops a formal policy this school year. LAUSD had already banned devices before second grade and set screen-time limits as part of a broader policy adopted in June. Like Los Angeles, New York is pairing AI restrictions with broader limits on technology use. New York's new plan also includes recommended screen time limits – a cap of 30 minutes daily for grades three to five and 45 minutes for grades six to eight. The plan also calls for a citywide review of education technology tools to eliminate those deemed nonessential to learning. At least 37 states already have some form of official AI guidance for schools, according to the Associated Press, but no consistent national standard exists for AI literacy instruction. What has the reaction been? Reactions from education and advocacy groups were mixed. Michael Mulgrew, president of the United Federation of Teachers, welcomed the screen time limits but said the AI policy "leaves many questions unanswered," including how the Education Department will ensure the tools it purchases include adequate safeguards, AP reported. Landmark lawsuit against Meta kicks off in the US To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Josh Golin, executive director of the children's advocacy group Fairplay, told AP he wanted a longer moratorium and more lead time before the school year began, adding that AI platforms should have to "demonstrate that their products are effective at teaching kids, that they're safe, that they're not displacing face-to-face interaction and that they're not leading to rampant cheating." "A year to evaluate is not nearly enough time," he said. New York City's roughly 1 million public school students return to classrooms next week. Kyiv told Bucharest the vessel was not Ukrainian, while Romania’s president blamed Russia. by Kyiv Post | Aug. 21, 2026, 3:35 am Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Romanian President Nicușor Dan at the Eastern Flank Summit in Gdansk, Poland, June 25, 2026. (Photo by Wojtek RADWANSKI / AFP) Romania scrambled two F-16 fighter jets on Thursday to destroy an explosive-laden marine drone detected near the Neptun Deep offshore gas project in the Black Sea, Romanian officials said. The small maritime drone was spotted in Romania’s exclusive economic zone near the Neptun Alpha platform, according to Romania’s Defense Ministry. One of the F-16s engaged the target with its onboard cannon and struck it. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Defense Minister Radu Miruță said the drone had approached within several hundred meters of the project and posed a danger to both critical infrastructure and hundreds of people working at the site. “In order to protect the lives of the several hundred people working on the platform and to secure critical infrastructure, the decision was made to destroy [the marine drone],” Miruță said. A vessel later reached the area and completed the drone’s destruction, the minister said, adding that it had been carrying explosives. Miruță did not initially identify who launched the drone. He said Romanian authorities contacted Ukraine through a newly established communication channel and Kyiv confirmed that the unmanned vessel did not belong to Ukrainian forces. Romanian President Nicușor Dan pointed to Russia as responsible for the incident, condemning what he described as an intensifying pattern of reckless Russian actions in the Black Sea. “I strongly condemn the intensification of these types of irresponsible incidents on the part of the Russian Federation,” Dan said, adding that Romania would remain vigilant alongside its NATO allies. Russia had not immediately commented. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the incident as part of what she called an “escalating campaign of threats.” Thursday’s incident comes amid growing concern over the security of energy and commercial infrastructure in the Black Sea as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues. Earlier in August, Romanian military divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones found drifting in Romania’s exclusive economic zone near the Neptun Deep area. Romanian naval specialists also recovered a drone wing near the Neptun Alpha platform on Aug. 16 after it was spotted by a commercial vessel. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP View image in fullscreen The secretaries board – which is chaired by Steven Kennedy (pictured) – said it was concerned about material from parliamentary hearings being presented online without proper context. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP Australian politics Australia’s top bureaucrats want to block sharing of clips from parliament on social media to save them from ‘ridicule’ Secretaries board concerned material posted without proper context as Greens warn ban could result in lack of transparency Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Sarah Basford Canales and Tom McIlroy Mon 7 Sep 2026 05.05 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 05.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The nation’s top bureaucrats want the Albanese government to ban video footage from parliamentary hearings being edited and shared on social media, in an extraordinary attempt to stop online ridicule and abuse. But the Greens say highly paid public service chiefs shouldn’t be allowed to control footage from open parliamentary hearings, warning the proposed controls would limit a key tool of government transparency. The secretaries board – made up of the heads of government departments and chaired by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet boss, Steven Kennedy – said they were concerned about material from hearings being presented online without proper context. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Politicians and political parties doing so exposed officials to “ridicule, hostility and abuse”, the board said. “Recognising the evidence provided to a committee is on the public record, these officials have not consented to a subsequent use of their image, or its use by parliamentarians and their political parties for party-political purposes,” the board said in a submission published on Monday. “In our view, the use of officials’ likenesses and their evidence in this way has the potential to be harmful both to the individual and the public sector as a whole.” If the recommendations are not taken up, the board called for rules that would stop videos being edited or having captions added. Politicians would also be stopped from sharing content or commentary that targets individual officials for ridicule or harassment. That sound you hear is not the world ending – it’s liberalism being monstered | Waleed Aly Read more Calling for footage of full hearings and transcripts to be made available instead of clips, and for comments to be disabled, the board said its proposal would ensure “that scrutiny remains focused on evidence, administration and accountability rather than becoming personal”. The proposal also includes concerns that members of parliament might not have a clear understanding of the role and responsibilities of public servants, when compared with government ministers. The board called for clearer explanation, including for newer MPs. The push comes after the defence department deputy secretary Celia Perkins told a parliamentary hearing last week that public servants giving evidence did not consent to footage being shared on social media. “They do not consent to the reposting of our evidence to social media sites or the reproduction of our likenesses for the purposes outside the framework of the parliament and the transparent public proceedings of this committee,” Perkins said. The Senate foreign affairs, defence and trade committee rejected Perkins’ request on the advice of the Senate clerk. Greens senator Steph Hodgins-May told Guardian Australia that members of the public had the right to see footage from hearings into government scrutiny. “Bureaucrats shouldn’t get to decide where to draw the line on parliamentary scrutiny, particularly when they’re the ones being scrutinised,” she said. “Of course debate should be respectful, but restricting what parliamentarians can post from public proceedings is not the answer. “This looks like an attempt to take the teeth out of parliamentary scrutiny. Australians deserve more transparency and accountability, not less. And frankly, if this scrutiny wasn’t having an impact, they wouldn’t be so worried about it.” The secretaries board includes all departmental chiefs, the Australian Public Service commissioner and the chief executive of the National Indigenous Australians Agency. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘Carney’s presence in Strasbourg made the EU look more desirable globally than it sometimes appears to angry European electorates.’ Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen ‘Carney’s presence in Strasbourg made the EU look more desirable globally than it sometimes appears to angry European electorates.’ Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock Opinion European Union Opening the EU door for Canada is a harmless gesture. But it won’t fix Europe’s security crisis Paul Taylor Beyond the morale boost and Mark Carney’s stardust, ‘associate membership’ means little Thu 17 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 03.31 EDT Share Ursula von der Leyen brought a new mascot to her annual State of the Union address to the European parliament: the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney. The leader of a plucky, like-minded liberal democracy, locked in an unsought trade war with its much bigger bully of a neighbour, Carney crossed the Atlantic and attended this flagship event of Europe’s political calendar to demonstrate his country’s shared values and desire to get closer to the EU. He was rewarded with a standing ovation and the first ever offer of an (invented) status of “associate member” of the EU. The grand-sounding title is more a gesture of political support and reciprocal affection than any sort of binding engagement. The EU doesn’t have associate membership in its founding treaties. It does make association agreements with close countries, some of which eventually join the bloc. It also has partnership, trade and cooperation agreements with more distant friends – it had one with Russia, in happier times. But using the “m” word in connection with Canada , which fails the geographical test for membership, may create an ambivalent precedent for the many Balkan and eastern European countries that are actually negotiating to join the bloc – and for the UK, which stormed out a decade ago but is now eager to get closer again. Ukraine railed against any such “associate” status in May, when the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, floated the idea as a stepping stone towards eventual full EU membership. Western Balkan states that have been waiting more than two decades for accession want nothing to do with such a halfway house. For Canada, though, the honorific title conveys a sense of European solidarity in its struggle with Donald Trump’s US, and a degree of closeness on fundamental values that responds to Carney’s seminal call at Davos in January for an alliance of like-minded “middle powers” to uphold as much as possible of the rules-based international order. Carney’s presence in Strasbourg, and his applause for EU free trade, tech regulation and defence initiatives, made the EU look more desirable globally than it sometimes appears to angry European electorates tempted to vote for Eurosceptic populists in national elections next year. Von der Leyen must be hoping that a little of the Canadian prime minister’s stardust will rub off on the embattled European integration project, which faces headwinds not only from predatory great powers and hostile big tech but also from recalcitrant governments loth to share power and pool sovereignty in sensitive fields such as defence. Closer cooperation with Canada and other like-minded powers such as India, Japan, Australia and New Zealand can amplify the EU’s global influence and help build alliances in defence of democracy, open rules-based trade and security of supply for critical raw materials. However, it cannot mitigate the urgent threats that Europe faces from increasingly reckless Russian aggression, nor be a substitute for a vengeful US that under Trump seems hell-bent on disengagement from European security. View image in fullscreen Ursula von der Leyen delivers the annual State of the European Union speech in Strasbourg, 16 September, 2026. Photograph: Pascal Bastien/AP Von der Leyen offered three initiatives to address these challenges. She proposed a new EU mechanism, aligned with Nato’s article 4 security consultations, to enable countries to trigger urgent EU consultations if they fall victim to so-called hybrid warfare – cyber-attacks, drone incursions, undersea cable cutting, railway sabotage, energy grid disruption and disinformation campaigns. It was time for a “counter-hybrid playbook”, she said, in which the EU moved beyond just boosting resilience and took a more robust approach to responding to covert warfare. Whether all member states have the stomach to risk escalation by hitting back at Russia, even if such hybrid attacks start causing casualties, remains to be seen. EU and Nato members that have offensive cyberwarfare capabilities could and should be striking back now to set red lines for Moscow, for instance by putting Russian energy grids or airports out of action as a warning. But these are national measures unlikely to be aired or jointly approved in Nato or EU councils. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion European countries have gone beyond sanctions to put Russia’s shadow fleet of rust-bucket oil tankers out of action – impounding them on safety or insurance grounds, as France and the UK have done episodically , and denying them passage through sensitive straits. But each action must be thought through, to achieve a deterrent effect rather than inviting ever bolder defiance by Vladimir Putin that could spiral into a wider war. Von der Leyen’s other initiative, to be detailed in an updated European security strategy due next month, was to call for a European security council – including Ukraine, the UK and Canada alongside EU powers – to steer the continent’s expanding defence effort. Such a coalition of the willing, as I have advocated , could indeed provide top-level leadership and a crisis-management forum. The challenge will be to give it real levers of power, and avoid it becoming a talking shop. Von der Leyen’s Canadian caper is welcome because it shows we have friends willing to link their destiny to ours in troubled times. But it is not in itself a solution to the continent’s urgent security problems. Log in here » WARSAW, Poland (AP) — Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned on Thursday that Russia is planning hybrid strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland. Russia will pretend the attacks are “accidental” in order to “paralyze or at least weaken the motivation of NATO countries” to rush to the defense of the member state coming under attack, Tusk said in a speech to the Polish parliament. “There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the eastern flank and even cause destruction,” Tusk warned. FILE - Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk looks on during a press conference during the E5 summit of leading European nations ahead of the upcoming NATO summit, in Berlin, Wednesday June 24, 2026. (Kay Nietfeld/dpa via AP,File) “The official narration will be that it’s an accident and there is no reason for NATO to think about a response,” he added. He said Russia was more dangerous because it was increasingly using jet-powered drones, which fly higher and faster and thus are more difficult to detect by air defense before reaching their targets. Tusk has been for months warning that Russia might be preparing a more serious hybrid attack against a NATO country. His warnings have gotten increasingly specific as he received intelligence from NATO, Ukrainian and U.S. secret services, including the CIA, he said. In recent days, Tusk has said Russia was now focusing on attacking border crossings between Ukraine and its European neighbors in order to disrupt delivery lines to Ukraine. Four such incidents happened on Poland’s border with Ukraine in the past week and several others took place in the last weeks on Ukraine’s border with Moldova. Tusk said at the moment Russia was not ready for any peace talks “without the total capitulation of Ukraine.” “They are convinced the winter will be tragically critical for Ukraine,” Tusk said. He said last winter Poland stepped in with deliveries when Ukraine’s energy infrastructure came under attack, but if border crossings are destroyed, it will be much harder for Warsaw to offer such help this upcoming winter. “Russia’s goal is to destroy as much as possible the economy and logistics of Ukraine,” Tusk said, adding that intelligence indicates continuous attacks of “very high frequency and intensity” on six main Ukrainian cities should be expected in the near future. Tusk announced on Thursday he would travel to Ukraine overnight to Friday, in what can be seen as an act of defiance against Russia after European leaders narrowly escaped a drone strike on a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border on Sunday. Officials usually keep their travel plans to Ukraine secret for security reasons. In Kyiv, he said he would discuss with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy how to defend against the new types of drones as well as discuss with partners including Slovakia about further sanctions against Russia. On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that “major progress is being made toward establishing a U.S. Army base in Poland” after a U.S. delegation was in Poland last week to visit several possible locations. “If this happens, the location will be announced very soon,” Trump wrote. “This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance.” Poland has for years sought to host a permanent U.S. base as a strong guarantee of its security in the face of the rising Russian threat. Poland’s high defense spending and major U.S. arms purchases have persuaded the Trump administration to consider putting a permanent base in Poland even as it reorganizes and reduces its overall military presence in Europe. In May, the U.S. unexpectedly withdrew troops from the total of around 10,000 stationed in Poland, causing confusion among European allies and nervousness in Warsaw. But officials in both Poland and the U.S. soon said the withdrawal was temporary and Poland was not expected to suffer from the U.S. troop reorganization. https://hungarytoday.hu/the-simpsons-ani.text: “The Simpsons” Animator Gábor Csupó Opens Memorial Room at Budapest’s ORIGO Studios A new memorial room dedicated to world-renowned Hungarian-American animator Gábor Csupó has opened at ORIGO Studios in Budapest, celebrating a career that spans Hungarian animation and some of the most recognizable television productions of the past several decades. The exhibition is more than just a traditional museum display: in addition to original artifacts, personal items, and stories about his creative process, the presence of the artist himself, who remains active today, adds a personal dimension to the exhibition. Gábor Csupó. Photo: Hungary Today At the opening, the two-time Primetime Emmy Award winner, 15-time Emmy Award nominee, and Kossuth Prize laureate personally unveiled the exhibition, which traces his career from its beginnings at Pannónia Film Studio to the founding of Klasky Csupo Studio in the United States. Gábor Csupó’s work has influenced several generations of television animation; his name is associated with productions such as the early television episodes of The Simpsons, Rugrats, Aaahh!!! Real Monsters, The Wild Thornberrys, Rocket Power, and Duckman. As a film director, he became known for Bridge to Terabithia, Immigrants, and The Secret of Moonacre . The memorial room offers a glimpse into the creative decisions made at the drawing table, the process of building creative teams, and the importance of music in his work. Dr. Márta Fekszi Horváthné, CEO of ORIGO Film Group Zrt., emphasized at the opening that the exhibition pays tribute to a Hungarian artist who proves that the history of Hollywood is also the history of Hungarian artists. For ORIGO Studios, the exhibition is also a professional mission that, in addition to preserving cinematic heritage, aims to provide tangible inspiration to young people preparing for a career in the industry, demonstrating that the path from a sketch and an idea to an international audience can still be built today, the Budapest Reporter noted. Photo: Hungary Today Csupó also revealed to Hungary Today that his favorite item in the exhibition is the Simpsons jacket, which attracts attention whenever he wears it and which he particularly wanted to see included in the exhibition in Hungary. The animator played a key role in giving the characters their distinctive yellow skin color and Marge Simpson her vibrant blue hair. https://www.aol.com/articles/billionaire.text: Faizan Farooque Mon, September 28, 2026 at 12:17 AM UTC 0 Ron Baron has already earned billions from Elon Musk. Now the billionaire investor feels the largest portion of that gamble may still be in front of him. The founder of Baron Capital made a very positive case for SpaceX on a CNBC “Squawk Box” appearance , suggesting that reducing launch costs, on top of Starlink growth, and accelerating artificial-intelligence demand may drastically raise the company’s long-term worth. Baron said Baron Capital has invested roughly $25 billion in SpaceX and more than $5 billion in Tesla (TSLA) . Of the approximately $71 billion in profits he said the firm has generated for clients over its history, roughly $30 billion came from investments associated with Musk. His newest prediction about SpaceX is far broader. Ultimately, Starlink could be producing something like $1 trillion per year in sales and $700 billion to $800 billion in EBITDA, Baron said. Based on his assumptions, he said the satellite business itself could eventually be worth something like $14 trillion to $15 trillion. Those statistics are estimates from Baron, not financial forecasts from SpaceX. But advancements at both SpaceX and Tesla are providing investors with much more real data points to judge the Musk enterprises. Ron Baron sees a massive opportunity beyond SpaceX rockets Baron’s thesis for SpaceX starts out with one critical variable: the cost of reaching orbit. Reusable rockets have dramatically cut launch costs compared to the economics of traditional, expendable launch vehicles, he said. He expects Starship will drive those costs down even further, potentially making space accessible to businesses for which that wasn’t economical before. Starship is a fully reusable transportation system designed by SpaceX to carry more than 100 metric tons to orbit in a reusable configuration. That’s significant because Baron isn’t just predicting more rockets to launch. It is based on what cheaper launches allow. The most established example is Starlink. Baron said he had modeled the satellite network growing dramatically over the next decade, with consumer broadband accounting for only part of the potential revenue opportunity. Government customers, businesses, and mobile connectivity could contribute substantially more, he argued. And increasingly, Baron believes, AI agents could create another wave of communications demand as autonomous software performs more tasks around the clock. SpaceX’s own current plans illustrate how aggressively it is trying to expand network capacity. Starship will allow much more network capacity to be deployed per launch, and the company said its next-generation V3 Starlink satellites are expected to provide far more capacity than today’s generation. SpaceX is also no longer restricted to private-market holdings. The company priced its massive public offering in June at $135 per share, selling about 555.6 million Class A shares and raising roughly $75 billion. The stock began trading under the ticker SPCX. That gives public-market investors a direct way to judge whether SpaceX can grow into anything resembling Baron’s enormous long-term expectations. “We’re going to make hundreds of billions in the next 10 years from Elon,” Baron said. Related: Elon Musk sends strong message to SpaceX and Tesla investors The $15 trillion figure isn’t the most ambitious part of his thesis, either. Baron believes orbital computing could eventually create an even larger opportunity. SpaceX’s AI data-center plan strengthens Baron’s thesis One theme Baron kept returning to throughout the interview was space-based data centers . AI companies are demanding larger and larger amounts of computing infrastructure, which requires electricity, cooling, land, and significant capital. Some of those constraints could eventually be eased by moving computing infrastructure into orbit, says Baron. He said he expects SpaceX to begin deploying data center capability into space as early as 2027, though he said the timeline could slip. As for the new business, he called it “Star Mind” and said it could one day be bigger than Starlink. SpaceX has since publicly documented the underlying project, unlike some of Baron’s more aggressive financial assumptions. SpaceX says StarMind is a system of satellites in orbit that carry AI-compute hardware powered by solar energy. Its initial AI1 satellite design calls for up to 250 kilowatts of peak computing power, and SpaceX says a planned manufacturing facility in Bastrop is meant to support production of thousands of AI satellites starting as soon as late 2027. SpaceX also says Starship is key to that strategy because the company will need to launch large amounts of computing hardware at a reasonable cost. Its current planning assumes that the gradual deployment of millions of tons of satellites could result in a huge amount of AI-compute capacity in orbit. These are company ambitions , not guaranteed outcomes, and building such infrastructure will require advances in launch cadence, satellite manufacturing, computing hardware and thermal management. Heat management is one of the challenges Baron discussed in the CNBC interview Hardware in space can’t use air-based cooling like ground-based data centers do. Instead, SpaceX’s StarMind design uses radiative cooling, solar power and laser links to tie the orbital compute network to Starlink. There is an official SpaceX orbital-AI program, which gives Baron’s larger argument a more concrete grounding. His valuation for Starlink is still very speculative at $14 trillion to $15 trillion. But the notion that SpaceX wants to be more than a rocket-and-internet company is no longer theoretical. Musk’s next growth engine could come from an unlikely placeBloomberg / Getty Images Tesla’s latest autonomy push backs part of Baron’s argument SpaceX may be Baron’s biggest bet on Musk, but Tesla is still a big part of his portfolio. Baron said his firm has more than $5 billion in Tesla stock, and he personally owns about $1.5 billion worth of the EV maker. Advertisement And he also cleared his stance on the shares. Baron said he believes “the time to buy the stock is now,” arguing that Tesla’s Full Self-Driving technology is gaining traction. Some recent data from Tesla also backs up the specific autonomy trends Baron pointed to, but it doesn’t prove his investment conclusion will be right. Tesla delivered 480,126 vehicles in the second quarter of 2026, including 467,762 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles. The company produced 451,758 vehicles and delivered 13.5 gigawatt-hours of energy-storage products in the quarter. Tesla’s financials included revenue of $28.24 billion for the second quarter, with net income attributable to common shareholders of $1.11 billion. The company said its strategy increasingly centers on bringing AI into the physical world through FSD, Robotaxi and humanoid robots such as Optimus. More Elon Musk: Elon Musk makes bizarre claims about money, future of AI Elon Musk sends blunt verdict on the future of humanity and AI Elon Musk’s startling claim to SpaceX investors Tesla’s Robotaxi operation has progressed further since that quarterly report. The current Robotaxi website for the company lists autonomous ride service in Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando and Tampa. Tesla claims the Cybercab is designed for full autonomy with no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla says Cybercab is now only available to take rides in limited areas of Austin , while Model Y vehicles support Robotaxi service in other markets. On Sept. 22, Tesla published a specific Cybercab rider guide explaining how customers can hail and ride driverless Cybercab rides via its Robotaxi app. Tesla is also making strides on FSD (full self-driving) outside of North America. On its FSD safety page, the European version currently lists the Netherlands, Lithuania, Estonia, Denmark, Belgium, Slovenia and the Czech Republic as markets where FSD (Supervised) has been approved. The system still needs driver supervision and should not be confused with a fully autonomous product. But Tesla’s push toward autonomy also faces regulatory scrutiny. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an investigation Sept. 4 into Tesla’s self-certification of the Cybercab after it began commercial deployment in Austin. The agency said it is looking into whether the vehicle complies with applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards. This is a necessary counterweight to Baron’s enthusiasm. FSD subscriptions and Robotaxi deployment are growing, but regulatory approval, technological reliability, and consumer adoption are key variables in how valuable those businesses ultimately become. Baron is not focusing as much on Tesla’s Optimus humanoid robot business. Musk believes robots could one day be bigger than Tesla’s other businesses, Baron said. But at the moment, Baron places more emphasis on autos, self-driving, batteries, and energy. That makes his investment thesis somewhat narrower than Mr. Musk’s own vision for Tesla. But it also connects directly to what Tesla is doing today: the rapid growth in adoption of FSD, the expansion of the Robotaxi service, and the move of Cybercab from development into the real world. Baron’s Musk bet is becoming an AI infrastructure bet Baron started wagering on Musk with electric cars and rockets. It increasingly feels like a gamble on the AI infrastructure. Tesla is trying to make AI into physical products with autonomous cars and robots. SpaceX is bringing more satellite connectivity online and building up orbital computing infrastructure that could potentially provide AI models with lots of compute. Baron believes those trends could come together. AI agents require connectivity. You need to be connected to network capacity. The AI models need the computing power. And SpaceX has a launch platform that could deliver communications and compute infrastructure to orbit at an unprecedented scale. There are big expectations. Baron sees a path to a Starlink revenue run rate of about $1 trillion and a valuation of as much as $15 trillion. He thinks orbital AI computing could be even bigger in the future. Neither is guaranteed. To build that future, Starship launch rates, satellite production, customer adoption, and AI-compute demand will all have to increase steeply, and significant engineering and regulatory hurdles will have to be overcome. Tesla’s own unknowns lie in its efforts to transform ever more capable autonomous-driving technology into a mass-scale transportation business. Yet the latest twists make one aspect of Baron’s thesis easier to grasp. His Musk bet is no longer primarily about cars or rockets . More and more, it’s about controlling the infrastructure required to connect, move, and provide computing power for an AI-driven economy. And the opportunity is just beginning, says Baron. Photograph: Lee Hulsman/Getty Images New South Wales Ebike rider, 13, charged with sexual touching after girls and women allegedly harassed on northern beaches Sydney teenager charged with offensive behaviour and sexual touching without consent in relation to incidents involving females aged 13 to 54 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Penry Buckley Sat 17 Oct 2026 19.53 EDT Last modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 20.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An ebike riding 13-year-old boy has been charged with multiple sexual offences allegedly committed against women on walking trails on Sydney’s northern beaches. New South Wales police said the boy was arrested on Saturday evening after a strike force was established to investigate inappropriate comments and alleged sexual touching incidents on walking trails in the Narrabeen area in the first weeks of October. “Following a public appeal, a 13-year-old boy was arrested after attending Mona Vale police station about 7.30pm yesterday,” police said on Sunday. The teenager was taken to Manly police station and charged with three counts of behaving in an offensive manner in or near a public place, and eight counts of sexually touching another person without consent. On Saturday, police had released CCTV images of a male they believed could assist with inquiries. Police allege that 11 separate incidents occurred against girls and women aged between 13 and 54. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The investigation was initially launched after three separate alleged incidents on 7 and 8 October. “In each incident, a male allegedly approached women on walking trails, sexually touched them and then rode away on an ebike,” police said on Saturday. In one of the incidents, the offender allegedly made “inappropriate sexual comments”. At Narrabeen lagoon about 4.30pm on 1 October the suspect “allegedly sexually touched [a] woman before riding away on an ebike,” police said. Last Monday, police received a further report that between 5pm and 5.30pm that day, two women walking along the Narrabeen lagoon near Bilarong reserve had been sexually touched by a male riding an ebike. Strike Force Mexvo was established to investigate the incidents with assistance from state crime command’s sex crimes quad. Speaking in Narrabeen before Saturday’s arrest, Supt John Duncan urged members of the public to come forward with any information about the alleged incidents. “It’s a bushland park that runs 8km, a large amount of which … runs through bushland, obviously there’s not a great deal of CCTV and cameras.” The 13-year-old was granted conditional bail to appear at children’s court on 4 November.
